> [!TLDR]
> Shear changes a circle into an oriented ellipse through the symmetric tracefree part of the deformation tensor.

<!-- PDF page 50; printed page 34 -->

Suppose next that $\mechanical{B}^a{}_b$ is symmetric and tracefree, so that

$$
\mechanical{B}^a{}_b=\begin{pmatrix}
\mechanical{\sigma}_+&\mechanical{\sigma}_\times\\
\mechanical{\sigma}_\times&-\mechanical{\sigma}_+
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Then $\Delta\mechanical{\xi}^a=\mechanical{r}_0\Delta\mechanical{t}(\mechanical{\sigma}_+\cos\mechanical{\phi}+\mechanical{\sigma}_\times\sin\mechanical{\phi},-\mechanical{\sigma}_+\sin\mechanical{\phi}+\mechanical{\sigma}_\times\cos\mechanical{\phi})$. The parametric equation describing the new figure is $\mechanical{r}_1(\mechanical{\phi})=\mechanical{r}_0(1+\mechanical{\sigma}_+\Delta\mechanical{t}\cos2\mechanical{\phi}+\mechanical{\sigma}_\times\Delta\mechanical{t}\sin2\mechanical{\phi})$. If $\mechanical{\sigma}_\times=0$, this represents an ellipse with major axis oriented along the $\mechanical{\phi}=0$ direction (Fig. 2.2). If, on the other hand, $\mechanical{\sigma}_+=0$, then the ellipse's major axis is oriented along $\mechanical{\phi}=\pi/4$. The general situation is an ellipse oriented at an arbitrary angle. It is easy to check that the area of the figure is not affected by the transformation. What we have, therefore, is a shearing of the figure, and $\mechanical{\sigma}_+$ and $\mechanical{\sigma}_\times$ are called the *shear parameters*. These may also vary over the medium.
